Best NAS for Small Business (2026): 6 Office Picks | ComputingForGeeks

 Before you pick the best NAS for a small business, settle what the box actually has to do, because a small office rarely needs raw speed. It needs shared folders that respect Windows or Active Directory permissions, backups of every laptop, snapshots that ransomware cannot delete, and an offsite copy that runs without anyone remembering it. Hardware that handles all four quietly for five years is the goal, and that narrows the field faster than any benchmark.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 172410 
 We shortlisted six small business NAS units for offices of roughly 5 to 50 people, from a budget 4-bay file server to a short-depth rackmount and a ZFS appliance with no license fees. Every price, spec and drive policy below was checked against the manufacturer’s pages and live Amazon listings in October 2026, and the business features (domain join, immutable snapshots, high availability, backup targets) come from each vendor’s own documentation rather than the marketing pages. That matters this year, because Synology changed its drive rules twice and the result is more nuanced than “the lock is gone”.
 Best NAS for small business: quick picks
 Award Model Price band Why it wins 
 Best overall Synology DS925+ about $760 DSM’s full business stack, ECC RAM, third-party drives allowed again 
 Best for Windows and AD offices Synology DS1825+ about $1,480 8 bays (18 with expansion), 8 GB ECC, PCIe slot for 10GbE or 25GbE 
 Best budget QNAP TS-464 about $640 AD, quotas and a PCIe slot at the lowest price here, plus a ZFS OS option 
 Most hardware for the money UGREEN DXP6800 Pro about $1,100 Core i5, two 10GbE ports, six bays, 3-year warranty 
 Best rackmount Synology RS1221+ about $1,650 Short-depth 2U, 8 bays, High Availability support, no drive lock 
 Best ZFS with no license fees TrueNAS Mini X+ about $2,160 direct 32 GB ECC, dual 10GBase-T, IPMI, snapshot holds included 
 Prices are Amazon US on October 1, 2026, and they are moving during the 2026 memory and drive shortage, so treat each as a band and check the live price before you order. Drives are not included in any of them.
 How we picked
 We started from what a 5 to 50 person office asks of its file server and worked backwards, which ruled out a lot of popular home NAS boxes. A pick needed a domain join or LDAP integration, snapshot protection, a route to offsite backup, a vendor warranty of at least a year, and an Amazon listing sold and shipped in the US at a sane price. We verified specs on each manufacturer’s spec page, confirmed the exact Amazon listing and stock on the day, and read at least one independent review per model (BizTech, ITdaily, ITPro, NASCompares, ServeTheHome or StorageReview).
 We did not have these six units in the lab, so we do not quote throughput numbers of our own for them. Where software behaviour matters, we lean on vendor documentation and on testing we have done: our TrueNAS vs Unraid lab run injected real corruption into a ZFS pool and watched TrueNAS repair it, which is the behaviour the Mini X+ pick relies on. We dropped several candidates: the Asustor Lockerstor Gen3 and the Synology DS1525+ were only sold by third-party resellers, the new Synology neo+ series ships with non-ECC memory and was only listed through Amazon Japan, and two-bay models fall below what an office needs.
 Small business NAS comparison table
 Model Bays CPU RAM (max) Network / 10GbE path Immutable snapshots Warranty

 Synology DS1825+ 8 (18 with 2x DX525) Ryzen V1500B 4C/8T 8 GB ECC (32 GB) 2x 2.5GbE, PCIe slot Yes 3 years (5 with EW+) 
 QNAP TS-464 4 + 2 M.2 Celeron N5095 4C/4T 8 GB non-ECC (16 GB) 2x 2.5GbE, PCIe slot On QuTS hero 3 years 
 UGREEN DXP6800 Pro 6 + 2 M.2 Core i5-1235U 10C/12T 8 GB, no ECC (64 GB) 2x 10GbE, PCIe slot No (locked snapshots stay admin-deletable) 3 years 
 Synology RS1221+ 8 (12 with RX418) Ryzen V1500B 4C/8T 4 GB ECC (32 GB) 4x 1GbE, PCIe slot Yes 3 years (5 with EW+) 
 TrueNAS Mini X+ 5 + 2 SSD Atom C3758 8C 32 GB ECC (64 GB) 2x 10GBase-T + IPMI Snapshot holds (full admin can release) 1 year (3 optional) 
 Synology DS925+: best overall for most offices
 For an office of up to about 20 people that wants a file server it can forget about, the DS925+ is where we would start, mostly because of the software around it rather than the box itself:
 Synology DS925+: Ryzen V1500B, 4 GB ECC, 4 bays plus 2 M.2, dual 2.5GbE. Image: Synology. 
 DSM joins an Active Directory domain or Microsoft Entra Domain Services from Control Panel, applies domain users and groups to shared-folder permissions, and supports Windows ACLs over SMB. Btrfs shared folders can take immutable snapshots, which Synology says “cannot be removed by any means” until a protection period you set expires (it recommends 7 to 14 days). That is the single most useful anti-ransomware control a small office can turn on. Hyper Backup then sends an encrypted, block-level incremental copy to another Synology, an rsync server, Azure, an S3-compatible bucket or Synology’s own C2 cloud. The spec page rates it for 40 concurrent SMB connections and 512 local users.
 It fits offices of 5 to 20 people that want domain-aware file shares, laptop backup and ransomware-resistant snapshots on one box. Look elsewhere if you need 10GbE, because there is no PCIe slot and therefore no upgrade path, or if your workload needs more than the 4 GB it ships with (plan an upgrade for Synology Drive, Active Backup or VMs, and note Synology limits warranty support on non-Synology RAM). NVMe storage pools still require Synology SSDs. It is about $760 on Amazon, sold by Amazon itself; check the live price .
 Synology DS1825+: best for Windows and Active Directory shops
 Once an office grows past 20 people, or its data clearly will not fit in four bays within a couple of years, we would step up to the DS1825+ rather than buying a second small box. It runs the same DSM business stack as the DS925+ on eight bays, with 8 GB of ECC memory and a PCIe slot:
 Synology DS1825+: 8 bays (18 with expansion), 8 GB ECC, PCIe Gen3 slot for 10GbE or 25GbE. Image: Synology. 
 The slot is a Gen3 x8 connector with a x4 link, enough for a 10GbE or 25GbE card, and two DX525 expansion units take it to 18 drives. BizTech ran one as the primary file and backup server for a 10-person office for a month, and called out that Active Backup for Business does not charge per seat, which is a real cost advantage over per-device backup software. Synology rates it for 60 concurrent SMB connections and 1,024 local users, and it is on Synology’s list of models that support WriteOnce (WORM) shared folders as well as immutable snapshots.
 We would buy it for a Windows office of 20 to 50 users with a domain controller, or for anyone who wants room to grow without a migration later. It is the wrong box if you want to run VMs or heavier apps on the NAS, because the 2018-era V1500B has no integrated graphics and modest headroom, or if you would rely on the expansion units for performance (NASCompares found the DX525 link runs at USB 3.2 Gen 1 speed, 5 Gbps). It is about $1,480 on Amazon, sold by Amazon itself; check the live price .
 QNAP TS-464: best budget small business NAS
 The TS-464 is the cheapest box here that still checks the business boxes, and it is the only budget pick with a PCIe slot. At about $640 it undercuts the DS925+ by over $100:
 QNAP TS-464: Celeron N5095, 8 GB, 4 bays plus 2 M.2, dual 2.5GbE, PCIe slot. Image: QNAP. 
 QNAP’s QTS handles Active Directory membership, Windows ACLs, and user, group and folder quotas, and it snapshots volumes on a schedule as often as every five minutes. The PCIe Gen3 x2 slot takes a 5GbE or 10GbE card later. The bigger option is the operating system: the TS-464 can run QuTS hero, QNAP’s ZFS-based OS, which adds WORM shared folders and immutable snapshots. You have to choose at install time, because switching from QTS to QuTS hero later erases the drives and QNAP requires removing them first, and inline deduplication on QuTS hero wants at least 16 GB.
 For an office of 5 to 15 people on a tight budget that still wants domain integration and a 10GbE path, it’s the obvious pick. Pass on it if you need ECC memory or more than 16 GB, which is this model’s ceiling, or fast NVMe storage (its M.2 slots run at Gen3 x1). It had 257 reviews and sells for about $640, now through a third-party seller (STC Distributors) rather than Amazon, and it currently ships on a later date; check the live price and ship date .
 UGREEN DXP6800 Pro: most hardware for the money
 On paper, nothing else here comes close for the price: a 10-core Core i5-1235U, two 10GbE ports, six bays, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, a PCIe x4 slot and a 3-year warranty for about $1,100. It’s the box we’d pick for a creative studio that moves large files over 10GbE all day:
 UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Pro: Core i5-1235U, 2x 10GbE, 6 bays, 3-year warranty. Image: UGREEN. 
 The catch is the software, and for a business it is a serious one. UGOS Pro has an Active Directory option in its UI, but an independent test of UGOS found it behaves as an LDAP bind rather than a true domain-member join, so test it against your own domain controller before rolling it out (that test used FreeIPA, not Windows Server). UGREEN’s own backup guide says its locked snapshots “remain manageable by an administrator, so they are not immutable recovery copies”, which means a compromised admin account can delete them. UGREEN also advertises “ODECC”, which is DDR5’s on-die error correction, not ECC memory.
 The right buyer is a small studio or team that cares most about 10GbE throughput, or an IT-comfortable office that plans to install TrueNAS on it (UGREEN has said, according to NASCompares, that a third-party OS does not void the hardware warranty as long as it does not damage the hardware). Avoid it if you depend on domain membership, need immutable snapshots for compliance, or want vendor support for the whole stack. We compared it in depth against its closest rival in ZimaCube 2 vs UGREEN DXP6800 ; it’s about $1,100 on Amazon, check the live price .
 Synology RS1221+: best rackmount NAS for a server closet
 If the office already has a rack, the RS1221+ is the one we would put in it, and its age is part of the reason. It is a short-depth 2U chassis with eight bays, expandable to 12 with an RX418 unit, running the same V1500B and DSM as the desktop Plus models:
 Synology RackStation RS1221+: short-depth 2U, 8 bays, 4x 1GbE, PCIe slot, High Availability capable. Image: Synology. 
 Because it launched before 2025, Synology’s newer drive rules do not apply to it, so third-party hard drives work for new pools. Its 2026 successor, the RS1226+, and the 4-bay RS826+ both state “Compatible drives are mandatory” on their spec pages. It supports Synology High Availability, which pairs two identical units for automatic failover, and Synology rates it for 180 concurrent SMB connections. Pairing has strict conditions, though: identical models running the same DSM version with the same number of LAN ports, identical drives in identical slots, and no SHR or M.2 SSD pools on the active server.
 It belongs in an office with a rack, a closet away from desks, and a plan to add 10GbE through the PCIe slot. Keep it out of the room if people sit nearby (ITPro measured the redundant-PSU RS1221RP+ at 58.7 dB at one metre), or if you will not buy a 10GbE card from Synology’s compatibility list (ITPro’s unit refused to boot with a Broadcom card and only worked with an Intel one). Out of the box it is 4x 1GbE. It’s about $1,650 on Amazon, and the dual-PSU RS1221RP+ is about $2,150; check the live price . On a smaller budget, QNAP’s 1U TS-464eU costs about $850 but has no PCIe slot and no 10GbE path.
 TrueNAS Mini X+: best ZFS appliance with no license fees
 For data where silent corruption is unacceptable (accounting archives, legal files, design masters), we’d choose ZFS on ECC memory, and the Mini X+ is the turnkey way to get it from the company that makes TrueNAS:
 TrueNAS Mini X+: Atom C3758, 32 GB ECC, 5+2 hot-swap bays, 2x 10GBase-T, IPMI. Image: iXsystems. 
 It ships with 32 GB of ECC memory (64 GB maximum), five hot-swap 3.5-inch bays and two 2.5-inch SSD bays, dual 10GBase-T and a dedicated IPMI port for remote management. The software is TrueNAS Community Edition, whose feature list includes Active Directory, LDAP, SMB multichannel, SMB auditing, “unlimited and immutable snapshots”, replication and cloud sync, with no per-user or per-feature license. Those snapshots cannot be edited, but a full administrator can still delete them, so TrueNAS recommends running daily work under its Sharing Admin role, which can place a snapshot hold but cannot release one. When we corrupted a gigabyte of one disk in a RAIDZ1 pool on a TrueNAS VM in our lab, TrueNAS served every file intact and a scrub repaired 108 MB in 48 seconds. If AD is the plan, our guide to joining TrueNAS to Active Directory covers the setup.
 Choose it when data integrity comes first and someone on the team is comfortable with ZFS concepts. Think twice if you need vendor-grade support, because the default warranty is one year (three is optional), or modern CPU performance, since the Atom C3758 dates to 2017. High Availability is only in TrueNAS Enterprise, not on the Mini. The Amazon listing TrueNAS runs is currently unavailable, so buy it direct: the diskless Mini X+ with the one year warranty is about $2,160 in the TrueNAS configurator , where you can also add the three year warranty or order it with drives fitted. The alternative is TrueNAS on hardware you choose, which our DIY NAS vs prebuilt breakdown prices out.
 Synology’s drive policy in 2026: what changed and what did not
 This is the question most small business buyers ask first, and the honest answer depends on the model. In 2025, Synology required drives from its own compatibility list on new Plus models. In October 2025, DSM 7.3 relaxed that for 2025 DiskStation Plus models like the DS925+ and DS1825+: third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs can now create new storage pools. Two restrictions remain, and DSM 7.4 added a third. M.2 NVMe drives still have to be on Synology’s list for storage pools and cache. The 2025 and 2026 RackStation Plus models still require listed hard drives for new pools. DSM 7.4, released in June 2026, added hard-drive deduplication and compression that only works with Synology drives.
 Synology’s knowledge base also states the new policies “do not apply retroactively to previously launched systems”, and that clause is the reason the 2021 RS1221+ makes a better rack pick today than its successor. In practice this means a DS925+ or DS1825+ can take the same WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf drives you would put in any NAS. Our NAS hard drive picks cover which ones are CMR.
 What to look for in a small business NAS
 Directory integration that really joins the domain. If your users log in to Windows with domain accounts, the NAS should join that domain so permissions follow people rather than shared passwords. DSM, QTS and TrueNAS all do this; test UGOS before you depend on it.
 Snapshots that an admin cannot delete. QNAP warns that ransomware often goes after backups and snapshots first, using stolen admin credentials. Vendors use the word “immutable” for two different things, so check which one you are buying. Synology’s immutable snapshots and QNAP’s on QuTS hero cannot be deleted by anyone, admins included, until the protection period ends. TrueNAS snapshot holds stop day-to-day admins from deleting a snapshot, but a full administrator can release the hold. UGREEN’s locked snapshots stay deletable by any admin. Only the three Synology picks give you admin-proof snapshots out of the box; the TS-464 gets them once you switch it to QuTS hero.
 An offsite copy that runs itself. A NAS in the office is not a backup of the office. Schedule a nightly copy to a second NAS at another site or an S3-compatible bucket, and test a restore every quarter. Hyper Backup, QNAP’s HBS 3 and TrueNAS Cloud Sync all handle this.
 ECC memory where the data matters. The three Synology picks and the TrueNAS Mini ship with ECC; the QNAP TS-464 and the UGREEN don’t. For ZFS in particular, ECC guards against one of the few failure paths ZFS can’t catch itself: a bit flip in RAM before the checksum is calculated.
 A path to 10GbE, even if you do not need it today. Video editing over the network and full-machine backups are the first workloads to outgrow 2.5GbE. A PCIe slot (DS1825+, TS-464, RS1221+) or onboard 10GbE (DXP6800 Pro, Mini X+) keeps the box useful for its whole life, provided the switch can follow; our 10GbE managed switch picks cover that side.
 Warranty and support you will actually use. Three years is standard for Synology, QNAP and UGREEN’s 6-bay line, extendable to five on Synology in North America and Europe. TrueNAS Mini is one year unless you pay for three.

 Best NAS Case (2026): Mini-ITX to 12-Bay TrueNAS Chassis 
 Hardening the NAS before the office depends on it
 The box matters less than how it is configured on day one, and a few settings decide whether a ransomware incident is a bad afternoon or a lost year. This is the checklist we would run on any of the six before moving the office’s data onto it:
 Create a named admin account with two-factor authentication, then disable or rename the default admin. Day-to-day users never get admin rights.
 Protect every shared folder with snapshots on a 7 to 14 day protection period, hourly or daily. On Synology, turn on immutable snapshots. On QNAP, run QuTS hero and use immutable snapshots or WORM in Compliance mode. On TrueNAS, give daily admins the Sharing Admin role so they can place holds but not remove them. On the UGREEN, replicate to a second box with separate credentials.
 Set the minimum SMB protocol to SMB2 or later, and keep the admin web interface off the internet. Use a VPN or the vendor’s relay service for remote access instead of port forwarding.
 Configure the offsite backup job on day one and restore one folder from it to prove it works.
 Connect a UPS over USB so the NAS shuts down cleanly on a power cut; our UPS picks for a NAS cover sizing.
 Enable email alerts for drive health, failed logins and snapshot or backup failures, and send them to a shared mailbox rather than one person.
 Done in that order, the NAS that costs $640 and the one that costs $2,160 can give a small office the thing that matters most: a copy of yesterday’s files that an attacker can’t delete before you need it. On the Synology picks, and on the TS-464 under QuTS hero, that holds even if the attacker has the admin password. On TrueNAS, it depends on keeping the full administrator account out of daily use.

Best 8-Bay NAS for Media Libraries and Small Offices | ComputingForGeeks 
 Skip to content 
 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Eight bays is the point where the drives cost more than the NAS. Eight new 16TB WD Red Pro drives come to about $5,700. The boxes in this guide run from about $930 to $2,100 diskless, so the drives are 70 to 90 percent of every 16TB total we priced. Pick the 8-bay NAS for its CPU, network and warranty, then budget most of the money for disks.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 176358 
 We checked every price, seller and spec on October 21, 2026, against the maker spec sheets and the Amazon US listings. This is a spec-verified guide, not a hands-on test. The picks are split into two jobs: a big media library, where Quick Sync and capacity per dollar decide, and a small office, where ECC, ZFS or DSM and warranty length decide. For fewer drives, the 4-bay NAS guide covers the same ground one size down.
 8-bay NAS picks at a glance
 We ranked the six picks by job, with the diskless price band and the total once eight 16TB Red Pro drives are added. Usable space is the same 96 TB in RAID 6 on all of them, so the populated column is the real comparison:
 Pick Best for CPU Network ECC Box With 8x 16TB 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus Plex or Jellyfin library Core i5-1235U, Quick Sync 2x 10GbE No $1,350 to $1,400 about $7,100 
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G Cheap bulk storage ARM Alpine AL324 2x 10GbE SFP+, 2x 2.5GbE No $1,100 to $1,150 about $6,800 
 QNAP TS-873A-8G ZFS on a budget Ryzen V1500B 2x 2.5GbE, 10GbE by card Supported, ships non-ECC $1,400 to $1,450 about $7,150 
 Synology DS1825+ Windows and AD office Ryzen V1500B 2x 2.5GbE, 10GbE by card Yes $1,450 to $1,500 about $7,200 
 Synology DS1823xs+ Business-critical, 5-year warranty Ryzen V1780B 10GbE + 2x 1GbE Yes $2,000 to $2,100 about $7,750 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Rack in a UniFi network 4-core ARM Cortex-A57 2x 10G SFP+, 1x 10GbE No $930 to $960 about $6,650 
 Box prices differ by about $1,100 from the cheapest to the dearest. The spread between eight 12TB and eight 20TB drives is about $2,800, which is why the next section prices the drives before the box. All prices move during the 2026 shortage, so check the current price on Amazon before you order.
 How the numbers were collected
 Nothing here was benchmarked in our lab, so every figure has a source behind it. Each method below states where its numbers came from, and the sources file for this guide lists every page:
 Prices and sellers: the Amazon affiliate API on October 21, 2026, then a second check of the live product page with a US address, because the seller the API reports and the seller on the page disagreed for one pick.
 Specs: the maker spec page or datasheet first, then an independent review (ServeTheHome, NASCompares, ITPro, How-To Geek) where one exists.
 Usable capacity: RAID 6 keeps six of eight drives for data. The RAIDZ2 figure is 71.0 percent of raw, from the 8-wide row in our measured RAIDZ2 width table.
 Rebuild time: a floor computed as drive capacity divided by the maximum transfer rate in the WD datasheet, not a measured rebuild.
 Power figures are the makers’ own unless the text names a review, and not every maker says whether drives were fitted. The TS-832PX has no independent review at all, and the text says so where it matters.
 Step 1: Price the drives before the box
 New drives sold by Amazon itself came only from WD on the check date. Every new Seagate IronWolf Pro listing was a third-party seller with thin stock, and every Exos below $700 was renewed or recertified:
 Drive Per drive 8 drives RAID 6 usable Per usable TB 
 WD Red Pro 12TB $520 to $560 about $4,300 72 TB about $60 
 WD Red Pro 16TB $700 to $730 about $5,700 96 TB about $60 
 WD Red Pro 20TB $870 to $910 about $7,100 120 TB about $59 
 Seagate Exos X18 16TB, recertified $490 to $510 about $4,000 96 TB about $42 
 Cost per usable terabyte is nearly flat across the new Red Pro sizes: about $60 at 12TB and $59 at 20TB. Buy the capacity you need and not the size that looks cheaper per terabyte. The 12TB Red Pro is an air-filled drive rated at 34 dBA idle. The 16TB and 20TB helium models are rated at 20 dBA and draw 3.6 W idle against 6.1 W. In an office or under a desk, that makes 16TB the quieter floor.
 WD rates Red Plus for up to 8 bays and Red Pro for any bay count, so a full 8-bay box sits at the Red Plus ceiling. Red Plus is allowed, but Red Pro is the default we would buy for a box that runs office workloads around the clock. Our NAS hard drive guide ranks both by price per terabyte. Every drive here is CMR, which matters for the reasons in our CMR vs SMR explainer .
 Recertified drives cut the drive bill by about $1,700 on eight 16TB units. The trade is the warranty: the goHardDrive listing quotes a six-month Seagate replacement warranty, against five years on a new Red Pro. Our recertified drive guide covers when that trade makes sense, and a parity array with a second copy of the data is the case it fits.
 Step 2: Size the array for RAID 6 or RAIDZ2
 At eight drives of 12TB or more, RAID 6 or RAIDZ2 is the layout to run, because a rebuild reads every surviving drive end to end. The floor for that read, from the transfer rates WD rates them at, is half a day or more:
 Drive Rated max rate Rebuild floor RAID 6 usable RAIDZ2 reported 
 WD Red Pro 12TB 267 MB/s 12.5 h 72 TB (65.5 TiB) 68.2 TB 
 WD Red Pro 16TB 259 MB/s 17.2 h 96 TB (87.3 TiB) 90.9 TB 
 WD Red Pro 20TB 285 MB/s 19.5 h 120 TB (109.1 TiB) 113.6 TB 
 These floors assume the outer-track rate for the whole drive and no load from users, so real rebuilds run longer. A single-parity array spends that whole rebuild one drive failure from losing everything, which is the case against RAID 5 at these sizes.
 RAIDZ2 reports less space than RAID 6 for the same eight drives, 113.6 TB against 120 TB on 20TB disks, because of ZFS padding and the slop space ZFS reserves at the default record size. The full width table is in our RAIDZ2 drive count guide , where eight is also the widest vdev a single 8-port HBA can run.
 Eight 20TB drives also hit a Synology limit. Both Synology datasheets say a volume over 108 TB needs 32 GB of memory or more, and both boxes ship with 8 GB. A single 120 TB RAID 6 volume on either one means raising the RAM to its 32 GB maximum, or splitting the pool into two volumes.
 Step 3: Choose a box for a big media library
 A media library needs hardware transcoding for remote streams, enough network to move large files, and the lowest box price that still does both. Only one current desktop 8-bay box under $1,500 has an Intel iGPU with Quick Sync.
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus. About $1,350 to $1,400; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The DXP8800 Plus runs a 10-core Core i5-1235U with Iris Xe graphics, which gives it Quick Sync for Plex and Jellyfin. It ships with 8 GB of DDR5 (64 GB maximum), two 10GbE ports, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two NVMe slots, a PCIe x4 slot and a 128 GB boot SSD. UGREEN rates it at 70.39 W in access and 28.99 W with the drives hibernated, and sells it on Amazon itself.
 Drives: third-party drives are supported, with a compatibility list but no lock.
 Other operating systems: the UGREEN warranty page says the hardware warranty stays unchanged if you install a third-party system, which is why it is a common TrueNAS and Unraid box.
 Memory: the DDR5 is on-die ECC only. Intel lists no ECC support for the CPU, so this is not an ECC NAS.
 Warranty: 3 years under the UGREEN warranty policy, even though one block on the product page shows 2.
 Skip it if the data needs true ECC or a mature business suite. It is already the high-capacity pick in our Plex and Jellyfin NAS guide . The DXP Ultra guide covers the DXP8800 Ultra at about $1,750 to $1,800, which changes the CPU and the RAM ceiling (96 GB) and little else.
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G. About $1,100 to $1,150; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The TS-832PX is the cheapest desktop 8-bay box with 10GbE built in, with two 10GbE SFP+ ports and two 2.5GbE ports. Amazon sold it at about $1,100 to $1,150, with five left on the check date. QNAP rates it at 50.9 W typical and 27.9 W in standby with drives fitted.
 The CPU is a 4-core ARM Alpine AL324 at 1.7 GHz with 4 GB of non-ECC RAM in one slot (16 GB maximum), and it runs QTS only. That limits it to serving files: no transcoding, no ZFS, and little room for containers or VMs. Its single PCIe slot is Gen2 x2, and QNAP itself notes that a card there will restrict 10GbE performance. The warranty is 2 years, against 3 on the UGREEN, DS1825+ and TS-873A and 5 on the DS1823xs+. We also found no independent review of it. We kept it as a pick anyway. QNAP publishes full specs and power figures, and it is the only desktop 8-bay with 10GbE at this price.
 Anything on the box that needs a CPU rules it out. Buy it as a backup target or a bulk media share whose players do their own decoding.
 Step 4: Choose a box for a small office
 An office box is judged on what happens when something fails: ECC memory, a file system with snapshots, a warranty that covers the service life, and a supported upgrade path to 10GbE. Four picks cover that, from a budget ZFS box to a rack unit for UniFi sites.
 QNAP TS-873A-8G
 QNAP TS-873A-8G. About $1,400 to $1,450; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The TS-873A is the cheapest pick here with ZFS and an ECC-capable CPU. It runs a 4-core Ryzen Embedded V1500B with 8 GB of RAM (64 GB maximum). It boots QTS or QuTS hero, the QNAP ZFS system with snapshots and inline compression. Two PCIe Gen3 x4 slots take a 10GbE card and a second card; the onboard ports are two 2.5GbE.
 ServeTheHome measured 26 W idle with no drives and a 58 W maximum in its 2021 review, and QNAP rates it at 54.1 W typical with drives. The platform dates from 2021, and its two M.2 slots are Gen3 x1, so NVMe cache is slow. The stock 8 GB is not ECC. QNAP says ECC memory requires removing the pre-installed modules, because ECC and non-ECC cannot be mixed, so matched ECC SODIMMs are an extra cost on top of the box price. Price a 10GbE card from the QNAP compatibility list in from the start too, and plan for 16 GB of RAM for ZFS deduplication; ITPro recommends 32 GB for QuTS hero once 10GbE is added.
 Look elsewhere if you want ECC or 10GbE without extra parts, or fast M.2 storage.
 Synology DS1825+
 Synology DS1825+. About $1,450 to $1,500; check the current price and seller on Amazon. 
 The DS1825+ is the pick for an office that already runs Active Directory and wants DSM. It has the same Ryzen V1500B as the TS-873A, with 8 GB of ECC DDR4 (32 GB maximum) and two 2.5GbE ports. Two NVMe slots and a PCIe Gen3 slot with an x4 link for a 10GbE or 25GbE card complete it. Two DX525 expansion units take it to 18 bays, and Synology rates it at 60.1 W in access.
 On DSM 7.3 or later, the 2025 Plus models accept unlisted hard drives for new pools again. Unlisted M.2 drives are still limited to migration, with no new pool or cache, so buy Synology SSDs if you want NVMe cache. The full policy is on the Synology drive compatibility page , and our Synology alternative guide compares it with the other vendors.
 On the check date, the page seller was RockyStone Electronics, a third party, at about $1,450 to $1,500. The Amazon catalogue listed Amazon as the merchant at the same time. Check who sells it before you order, and buy from an authorized Synology reseller if warranty support matters. Our small business NAS guide covers the DSM and AD setup, and the neo+ vs Plus comparison covers the cheaper DS1825neo+.
 Synology DS1823xs+
 Synology DS1823xs+. About $2,000 to $2,100; check the current price on Amazon. 
 About $600 more than the DS1825+ buys three things: a 5-year warranty, a faster 4-core Ryzen V1780B, and 10GbE on the board next to two 1GbE ports and a management port. It has 8 GB of ECC memory (32 GB maximum), the same Gen3 slot with an x4 link, and 18 bays with two DX517 units. Synology rates it at 87.93 W in access. Amazon sells it directly.
 As a 2023 xs model, it is outside the 2025 drive policy change, because Synology says that change does not apply retroactively. Owners report “unverified” warnings in DSM when they fit third-party drives. It also has no SHR, only standard RAID levels.
 Pass on it if you plan to fill it with WD or Seagate drives and do not want those warnings, or if anything needs transcoding.
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8. About $930 to $960 from a third-party seller on Amazon; check the current price. 
 UniFi built the cheapest box here and the only rack unit among the picks: 2U, 480 mm deep, with rails in the box. It has two 10G SFP+ ports and one 10GbE RJ45 port, a 4-core ARM Cortex-A57 with 16 GB of soldered RAM, and two hot-swap power supply bays. NASCompares measured about 800 to 850 MB/s sequential read from eight 8TB drives in RAID 5.
 Price: Ubiquiti lists it at about $800 before a checkout surcharge. On Amazon it comes from a third-party seller at about $930 to $960 on October 21, 2026; check the current price.
 Power: one 550 W supply is included, and the second for redundancy costs about $159.
 Storage: RAID 5, 6 or 10 with a hot spare, shared over SMB and NFS. There is no iSCSI and no app or container platform, and the trays for its two M.2 cache slots are sold separately.
 Warranty: the UI Store page lists no base term, only UI Care, which extends cover to 5 years for about $199. US resellers list a 1-year limited warranty, which would make it the shortest base cover here.
 Skip it if you need Docker, iSCSI, ECC or any software outside UniFi Drive. Buy it if the rack already holds UniFi gear; our first rackmount server guide covers depth and rails for a home rack.
 Step 5: Price a DIY 8-bay build
 A DIY build with Quick Sync and eight SATA ports on the board costs about the same as the DXP8800 Plus at current DDR5 prices. This basket uses a Jonsbo N3 case and a Mini-ITX board with eight SATA ports, so no HBA is needed:
 Part Pick Band 
 Case Jonsbo N3, 8 hot-swap bays about $160 
 Board StoneStorm Q670 Mini-ITX, 8 SATA about $210 
 CPU Intel Core i5-14400 about $210 
 Memory Crucial Pro 2×16 GB DDR5-6000 about $540 
 Power Cooler Master V750 SFX Gold about $125 
 Boot WD Green SN3000 500 GB about $95 
 10GbE TP-Link TX401 about $60 
 We priced the basket at about $1,400 for 32 GB of RAM, against 8 GB in the DXP8800 Plus at about the same price. A lean version with 16 GB and a Core i3-14100 comes to about $1,050 to $1,100, though the i3 was listed for a later ship date. Several parts were sold by third parties with thin stock. The specs for the board come from its Amazon listing only, and that listing does not state the PCIe slot, so confirm it before you buy the 10GbE card.
 DIY no longer saves money at this size, so build one for the freedom to run any OS. Unraid at eight drives also needs its Unleashed licence, about $109, on top of the basket. There is also no ECC on a Q670 board. The case options are in our NAS case guide , the power and cost comparison is in DIY NAS vs prebuilt , and the OS choice is in TrueNAS vs Unraid .
 Step 6: Match the network to the array
 Eight hard drives in a parity array read faster than a 2.5GbE port can carry. NASCompares measured 800 to 850 MB/s from eight 8TB drives in RAID 5 on the UNAS Pro 8. A 2.5GbE link tops out near 280 MB/s, so a 2.5GbE-only box leaves most of the array idle on large transfers.
 10GbE on the board: DXP8800 Plus, TS-832PX, DS1823xs+ and UNAS Pro 8. On the DXP8800 Ultra, ITPro measured 9.2 Gbit/s read and 8.8 Gbit/s write in the Iometer synthetic test, and 3.8 and 3.0 Gbit/s copying a 25 GB file.
 10GbE by card: TS-873A and DS1825+. Use a card from the QNAP or Synology compatibility list for each box.
 The switch: a 10GbE NAS needs a 10GbE port at the other end, which our 10GbE switch guide covers.
 A 1GbE or 2.5GbE network is fine for streaming, because a single 4K stream needs a small fraction of either. The 10GbE port pays off on backups, video editing and VM storage, and the box belongs on a UPS whichever network it runs, as our NAS UPS guide explains.
 Models we left out and why
 Several 8-bay boxes looked right in a search and failed a check. Each one is excluded for a specific, verifiable reason:
 QNAP TS-855X: the Amazon title says 8 bays, but the box has six 3.5-inch bays and two 2.5-inch bays.
 Synology DS1821+: discontinued. Its US product page now redirects to the download center, and the remaining Amazon listings are third-party bundles above $3,700.
 Asustor Lockerstor 8 Gen3 (AS6808T): true ECC and 10GbE, but about $1,820 or more everywhere, third-party only on Amazon, and no written independent review.
 TerraMaster U8-500 Plus: a 2U unit with a Core i7-1255U and 10GbE at about $1,530, but no independent review we could find, and its RAID grows only by swapping in larger drives, not by adding drives.
 TerraMaster U8-423: a 2U unit with a Celeron N5095 that does hardware transcoding, two 2.5GbE ports and a 2-year warranty, at about $825 direct from TerraMaster but not sold on Amazon US.
 TerraMaster F8 SSD: all-flash, covered in our all-flash NAS guide .
 QNAP TVS-h874 and TS-855eU: out of stock or used only on the check date.
 QNAP also previewed an 8-bay AI NAS at Computex in June 2026 without US availability, so it is not in this guide until it ships. Past eight drives, the next step is an expansion unit or a DAS or JBOD enclosure , not a bigger NAS.

 Cloud storage is convenient, sure, but monthly subscriptions can mount up exceptionally quickly, especially when your photo library, video collection, and backups continue growing relentlessly year after year.
 For many users, building a private cloud has become a practical alternative that provides greater control over data while eliminating recurring storage fees. That's where NAS comes in. Network-attached storage connects directly to your network, creating a centralized location for files, backups, media streaming, and remote access.
 Whether you're storing family photos, sharing documents across a small business, or managing large creative projects, a NAS can provide a secure and flexible storage platform.

 The good news is that setting up a private cloud no longer requires enterprise-level hardware or crazy, advanced knowledge. Modern NAS devices are easier to configure than ever, with intuitive software, mobile apps, and automated backup tools that handle much of the heavy lifting.
 For individuals looking to replace or supplement cloud services, the Ugreen NASync DXP4800 Plus offers a great starting point.
 It delivers plenty of performance for media libraries, personal backups, and home office use, while leaving room for future expansion.
 In his hands-on coverage of the product, our expert Mark said the "new NAS brand comes with serious intent" and that it was "exceptionally well-considered and powerful."
 Small businesses often require a little more flexibility, especially when multiple employees need access to shared files and backups.
 The TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is one of the most capable options in this category, combining fast hardware with business-friendly features that can support growing storage requirements.
 In his glowing review , Mark called it the "new powerhouse of the TerraMaster F4 series." He went on to say it was, "probably the most powerful 4-bay NAS available, the F4-424 Pro is ideal for those needing a development tool with plenty of processor performance."
 Professionals and demanding users managing larger workloads could benefit from stepping up to the Ugreen DXP4800 Pro.
 Mark's review called the model's arrive "timely" and said it provided a "subtle upgrade from the Plus model, yet these changes have significant implications for this network-attached storage device."
 With more processing power, higher memory limits, and support for advanced workloads, it can handle everything from virtualization to large-scale content storage.
 Of course, choosing the NAS itself is only part of the equation. Pairing the right enclosure with reliable drives can make a huge difference in performance, capacity, and long-term reliability.
 In this guide, we'll walk through the best NAS options for individuals, small businesses, and professional users, along with the storage drives we recommend to go with them for building a private cloud that fits your needs and budget.
 For more picks, check out our guides to the best NAS devices , best NAS hard drives and best NAS and media server distros .
 FAQ 
 Q: What is a NAS? 
 A NAS, or Network Attached Storage, is a dedicated storage device connected to a network that allows multiple users and devices to access files from a central location. It provides shared storage for documents, photos, videos, backups, and business data without requiring a full server setup.
 Q: Why would an individual user need a NAS? 
 Anyone with a growing collection of files can benefit from a NAS. It provides a private location for photos, videos, documents, and backups while making content available across computers, smartphones, and tablets. Many home users also use NAS systems for media streaming, remote access, and automatic backups.
 Q: What features are important for personal NAS systems? 
 Most personal users should focus on storage capacity, ease of setup, backup tools, and support for multiple drives. Features such as RAID protection, mobile apps, and cloud synchronization can provide additional convenience and data protection.
 Q: How does NAS benefit small and medium-sized businesses? 
 SMBs often need centralized file storage that employees can access from different locations. A NAS can simplify collaboration, automate backups, manage permissions, and reduce dependence on external storage devices. It also offers a more affordable alternative to dedicated servers for many organizations.
 Q: What should SMBs look for when choosing a NAS? 
 Businesses should consider scalability, user management, backup options, security features, and network performance. Support for virtualization, file versioning, and integration with business applications can also be valuable as storage requirements increase.
 Q: How does enterprise NAS differ from consumer and SMB solutions? 
 Enterprise NAS platforms are built for much larger workloads, higher performance requirements, and larger user counts. They often include advanced redundancy, failover protection, high-speed networking, and support for petabytes of storage.
 These systems are commonly deployed in data centers, large organizations, and environments where downtime isn't acceptable.
 Q: Is NAS secure? 
 Modern NAS systems offer encryption, user permissions, multi-factor authentication, and backup tools to help protect data. Security still depends on proper configuration, software updates, and strong access controls.
 Q: Can a NAS grow with changing storage needs? 
 Many NAS platforms support additional drives, expansion units, and capacity upgrades, allowing storage resources to increase as requirements change.
 Getting started 
 Getting started with a NAS device is easier than many first-time buyers expect and is essentially a dedicated storage system that connects to your home or office network, allowing multiple users and devices to access files from a central location.
 Before you begin, think about how you'll use it. Simple file storage and backups require less processing power than tasks such as media streaming, virtualization or surveillance recording.
 The next step is choosing the right hardware. Select a NAS enclosure with enough drive bays to accommodate both your current storage needs and future expansion.
 When selecting hard drives, look for models specifically designed for NAS environments, as these are built to handle continuous operation and multi-drive workloads.
 Consider using RAID for redundancy, which can help protect your data if a drive fails, although RAID should never be treated as a substitute for proper backups.
 Once your hardware is assembled, connect the NAS to your router and follow the manufacturer's setup wizard.
 Most modern NAS platforms provide straightforward web-based interfaces that guide you through creating storage pools, shared folders and user accounts. Be sure to enable automatic updates and configure backup jobs early in the process.
 With a little planning, a NAS can become the central hub for file storage, backups, media libraries and collaboration across your network.

 Best NAS for Small Business (2026): Compared, Ransomware-Resistant, Local vs Hybrid Cloud
 Reviewed by IT Cares certified technicians · Updated August 2026
 TL;DR — which NAS should a small business actually buy?
 For most small businesses, a 4-bay NAS with immutable snapshot support (Synology DS423+ or QNAP TS-464 class) paired with encrypted cloud replication is the right combination. RAID alone is not a backup — it only protects against a single drive failure. What actually stops ransomware from destroying your NAS along with your workstations is immutable snapshots plus a genuinely offsite copy, which is where a hybrid local-plus-cloud strategy comes in.
 Updated: August 2026 
 17 min read

 RAID protects against a dead drive. Immutable snapshots are what actually stop ransomware from reaching your backup history. 
 🗄️ 
 Not sure which NAS actually fits your business, or whether your current one is configured correctly? 
 Our certified technicians will assess your setup honestly and recommend what's actually right-sized.

 Most small businesses that own a NAS believe it's protecting them from more than it actually is. A box with two or four drives in RAID, sitting quietly in the server closet, feels like a solved problem — until a ransomware infection reaches the shared folder and encrypts every drive in the array at once, or a fire or break-in takes out the office and the "backup" sitting three feet from the workstation it was backing up.
 This guide is deliberately narrow: it's about the physical NAS hardware decision itself — which models make sense for a small business in 2026, what actually makes one ransomware-resistant versus just RAID-redundant, and how to combine it with cloud backup the right way. For the broader picture of business backup strategy — the 3-2-1 rule, Microsoft 365 backup gaps, and realistic Canadian cost ranges across every backup type — our cloud backup for business guide covers that ground in full. And if you're weighing NAS hardware against a fully managed backup service instead, our automated backups guide breaks down how that works and what it costs.
 Who wrote this guide
 This article was written and reviewed by IT Cares certified technicians based on selecting, configuring, and recovering NAS deployments for small businesses across Canada — including the calls that come in after a ransomware incident reached a NAS that had RAID but no immutable snapshots. We're not tied to one NAS brand — we're explaining what actually needs to be true about the hardware and configuration for it to protect a business when it matters.
 What Is a NAS, and Does Your Small Business Actually Need One?
 A NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a small dedicated storage server connected to your business network, with multiple bays to hold hard drives. Unlike a single external drive plugged into one computer, a NAS is reachable by every device on the network — Windows and Mac workstations, phones, tablets — and, configured correctly, from outside the office too.
 For a small business, the practical benefits are direct:
 Centralization — every company file lives in one place instead of scattered across eight different laptops
 RAID redundancy — if one physical drive fails, the data survives on the remaining drives
 Automatic workstation backup — every computer can back up to the NAS automatically (Time Machine for Mac, native Windows backup)
 Snapshots — point-in-time versions of your files you can roll back to in a few clicks
 Predictable cost — a one-time hardware purchase rather than a cloud subscription that climbs with every gigabyte added
 Secure remote access — remote employees reach the same files without relying entirely on a third-party service
 A NAS isn't the right fit for every business — if you'd rather keep everything in the cloud with no local hardware to manage, dedicated cloud backup covered in our automated backups guide may be the simpler path. But for a business handling meaningful file volume, local line-of-business software, or sensitive client data it wants direct control over, a NAS is usually the most cost-effective centerpiece of the setup.

 Here are the models we recommend most often, from tight budgets to growing businesses with dozens of employees. Prices below are for the chassis only, without drives.

 QNAP TS-464 4 bays 4GB (up to 16GB) Yes (QuTS hero/ZFS optional) $680–$780 Performance-focused SMBs, light virtualization

 Our general recommendation: for the large majority of the 5-to-25-employee businesses we work with, a Synology DS423+ or DS1522+ hits the best balance of manageable complexity, real immutable snapshot support, and cost. For a business with in-house IT that wants more technical control, a QNAP TS-464 running QuTS hero (ZFS) is often the more powerful choice at a comparable price.
 Be wary of prices that look too good
 A 4-bay NAS chassis under $300 almost always lacks sufficient RAM and doesn't support immutable snapshots — two things that actually matter for real small business protection. The chassis price is only part of the budget; don't sacrifice RAM and snapshot support to save $100-$150 upfront.
 Buying Checklist: What to Verify Before You Purchase
 Before settling on a model, run it through this list. A NAS that checks every box actually protects you; one that checks half of them mostly delivers a false sense of security.
 Checklist: what to look for in a small business NAS
 At least 4 bays (2-bay models only make sense for a solo operator or a 1-2 person team)
 Native immutable snapshot support (explicitly verify this — not just "snapshots," which many entry-level models offer without the immutability piece)
 Sufficient RAM: 4GB minimum, 8GB+ if multiple employees access the NAS simultaneously
 Btrfs or ZFS file system (required for immutable snapshots and data integrity checks)
 Native backup compatibility with both Windows and Mac (Time Machine, File History)
 At-rest encryption (AES-256) for sensitive data
 Built-in cloud replication or backup (Synology C2, Backblaze B2, or equivalent)
 Expandable (an expansion unit available if the business grows)
 Secure remote access via VPN or the manufacturer's gateway with two-factor authentication — never a NAS exposed directly to the internet unprotected
 At least a 2-3 year hardware warranty and available technical support
 Immutable Snapshots: The Real Ransomware Defense
 This is probably the most important section of this guide, because it's where most small businesses get it wrong. RAID is not a backup. If ransomware infects a workstation connected to the NAS and starts encrypting files on the shared drive, RAID will faithfully replicate those encrypted files across every disk — RAID protects against hardware failure, not against corrupted or encrypted content.
 That's exactly the gap immutable snapshots close. A snapshot is a point-in-time photograph of your files. An immutable snapshot (sometimes called "locked" or WORM — Write Once, Read Many) cannot be modified or deleted for a period you define, even by a compromised administrator account.
 How this actually stops a ransomware attack
 The NAS takes automatic snapshots at regular intervals (hourly or several times a day) and locks them as immutable for, say, 14-30 days
 Ransomware infects a workstation and starts encrypting files it can reach, including those on the NAS's network share
 Active files on the NAS get encrypted — but the locked snapshots from previous days remain untouched, since even an administrator account can't modify them during the lock period
 The technical team isolates the network, cleans the infection, and restores files from the last clean snapshot — usually within hours rather than days or weeks
 On recent Synology models (DSM 7.2+), this feature is called Snapshot Replication with the immutable lock option, available on Btrfs-formatted volumes. QNAP offers similar protection on models supporting QuTS hero (ZFS file system) with locked snapshots. Always check the specific model's datasheet before assuming this is included — it isn't universal across every entry-level model, even within the same brand.
 Minimum recommended configuration
 For a small business, we recommend hourly automatic snapshots during business hours, locked in immutable mode for at least 14 days. That window covers the large majority of real-world scenarios: most ransomware infections are detected within days of landing, rarely more than two weeks later.
 Local vs Cloud vs Hybrid: An Honest Comparison for NAS Owners
 Even a local NAS with immutable snapshots stays vulnerable to one scenario: a fire, theft, flood, or physical disaster at the office destroys both your workstations and the NAS sitting right next to them. That's why real protection always combines a local component with an offsite one.
 Strategy Protects Against Doesn't Protect Against Restore Speed 
 Local NAS only 
 Drive failure, accidental deletion, ransomware (with immutable snapshots enabled) 
 Fire, theft, flood at the office — total site loss 
 Fast (minutes to hours) 
 Cloud only (no local NAS) 
 Site disaster, hardware theft 
 Fully dependent on internet speed; recurring cost climbs with data volume 
 Slow for large volumes (hours to days depending on connection) 
 NAS + cloud replication (hybrid) 
 Nearly every scenario: drive failure, ransomware, disaster, theft 
 Higher setup complexity upfront 
 Fast locally, complete recovery via cloud copy after a total loss 
 The hybrid approach — a local NAS with immutable snapshots plus automatic, encrypted replication to a cloud service (Synology C2, Backblaze B2, or an equivalent provider) — is what we recommend to nearly all of our small business clients. In practice, that's the 3-2-1 rule applied concretely: your working copy (1), the local NAS (2, a different media type), and cloud replication (3, offsite). Our cloud backup for business guide covers the 3-2-1 rule in full depth if you want the broader picture beyond NAS hardware specifically.
 One important technical detail: cloud replication should use credentials separate from those used for day-to-day NAS access. If the same administrator account controls both the local NAS and the cloud copy, ransomware that compromises that account can potentially reach both. Always keep the access paths separate.
 Realistic Budget: What a NAS Actually Costs a Canadian Small Business
 The chassis is only part of the total cost. Here's a realistic breakdown by business size, in Canadian dollars.
 Very small business (1-5 employees): 2-4 bay chassis $300-$550, plus two NAS-rated drives (Seagate IronWolf or WD Red, 4TB each) at $250-$350, plus light cloud replication (a few hundred GB) at $8-$15 CAD/month. Initial budget roughly $550-$900, plus $10-15/month .
 Mid-size small business (10-25 employees): 4-5 bay chassis with immutable snapshots $630-$1,100, plus 4-5 NAS drives (4-8TB each, RAID 5/6) at $600-$1,200, plus cloud replication (1-3TB) at $20-$45 CAD/month, plus recommended professional setup $300-$800. Initial budget roughly $1,500-$3,000, plus $20-45/month .
 Growing business (25-75 employees, multiple offices or larger volumes): High-end expandable chassis, possibly paired for redundancy, $1,800-$4,000+; higher-capacity drives in redundant configuration $1,500-$3,500+; larger-volume cloud replication $60-$200+ CAD/month; setup, migration, and staff training $800-$2,500. Initial budget roughly $4,000-$10,000+, plus variable monthly costs .
 Compare these numbers against the average cost of a ransomware incident for a small business — frequently tens of thousands of dollars in lost productivity, emergency recovery, and sometimes ransom payment, not counting legal notification obligations if personal data was exposed. In that context, the NAS is rarely the expense a small business regrets making.

 Case Studies: Three Canadian Small Businesses and Their NAS Choice
 These illustrative scenarios reflect situations we see regularly across small businesses in Canada, showing how these criteria translate into real decisions.
 Case 1: Accounting Firm in Ottawa (9 employees)
 The firm ran client files off a seven-year-old Windows file server with no snapshots and a manual backup to an external drive done "whenever someone remembered." After hearing about a nearby firm hit by ransomware during tax season, leadership decided to act. They chose a Synology DS1522+ with 5 drives in RAID 6, hourly immutable snapshots retained 21 days, and encrypted replication to Synology C2. Six months later, an employee clicked an infected attachment on a Friday afternoon. Ransomware encrypted files on their workstation and part of the network share before being caught Monday morning. Because the snapshots were immutable, the technical team restored every client file from a snapshot taken the day before the infection — the real loss was a few hours of one employee's work, not weeks of client records.
 Case 2: Dental Clinic in Burlington, Ontario (6 employees)
 A dental clinic handling patient records subject to health privacy obligations was using a consumer cloud service with no additional encryption and no control over where the data physically lived. During a compliance review, the clinic moved to an on-premises Synology DS423+ with AES-256 volume encryption, named-user access with two-factor authentication, and an encrypted offsite copy. This gave the clinic direct, documentable control over where and how patient data was protected — a concrete point in favor during their compliance review, alongside removing a growing dependency on an expensive high-volume cloud subscription.
 Case 3: Design Studio in Vancouver, BC (14 employees)
 The studio works with large files (video, high-resolution assets) that made pure cloud backup painfully slow on their standard business internet connection. The team chose a QNAP TS-464 with 16GB RAM for fast local editing over the network, regular ZFS snapshots, and scheduled overnight cloud replication so it wouldn't compete for bandwidth during working hours. The result: fast local access and backup for day-to-day work, with offsite protection quietly happening during off-peak hours.
 What all three have in common
 None of these businesses bought "the most expensive" or "the most powerful" NAS. Each chose a model sized to its actual data volume, legal obligations, and workflow — then invested in configuring immutable snapshots and offsite replication correctly. It's the configuration, not just the hardware, that determines whether a NAS actually protects a business.
 Deployment: The Steps That Actually Matter
 A brand-new NAS out of the box provides no real protection until it's configured correctly. Here's what a proper setup should cover.
 1
 Configure RAID for the drive count
 RAID 1 for two drives, RAID 5 or 6 for four or more (RAID 6 tolerates two simultaneous drive failures — recommended for businesses that can't afford extended downtime).
 2
 Turn on immutable snapshots
 Schedule automatic snapshots (typically hourly during business hours) and set an immutable lock period of 14-30 days.
 3
 Set up cloud replication with separate credentials
 Connect to the chosen cloud service using an account distinct from day-to-day access, with encryption enabled before data leaves the device.
 4
 User accounts and permissions
 One named account per employee (never a shared login), permissions restricted to what each role actually needs, two-factor authentication required for every administrator account.
 5
 Secure remote access
 A VPN or the manufacturer's secure access gateway rather than exposing the NAS directly to the internet — a common mistake that turns a NAS into an easy target for automated attacks.
 6
 Test a real restore
 Restore a sample file from a snapshot to confirm the whole chain genuinely works — not just in theory. Repeat this test quarterly.
 How long this takes: for a mid-size business, a complete, secured setup typically takes between half a day and two days depending on the complexity of the existing network and the volume of data being migrated.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is a NAS and does my small business actually need one?
 A NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a small dedicated storage server connected to your business network with multiple drive bays. It centralizes company files in one place, lets every workstation back up automatically, provides RAID redundancy against a single drive failure, and gives secure remote access without relying entirely on a monthly cloud subscription. For a small business handling client files, financial records, or other sensitive data, it's often the most cost-effective way to have real, direct control over your data.
 Is RAID on a NAS the same thing as a backup?
 No, and this is one of the most expensive misunderstandings in small business IT. RAID protects against a single physical drive failing — if one drive dies, the other still holds your data. RAID does not protect against ransomware (which encrypts files across every drive in the RAID volume at once), accidental deletion, or theft or fire at the office. RAID is an availability measure, not a backup strategy — it needs to be paired with immutable snapshots and an offsite copy.
 What is an immutable snapshot and why does it matter against ransomware?
 An immutable snapshot is a locked, point-in-time copy of your files that cannot be altered or deleted for a set retention period, even by an administrator account. This is the critical defense against ransomware: modern ransomware actively searches for connected shared folders and backups to encrypt them too, but it cannot touch snapshots locked in immutable mode. If your snapshots are immutable, ransomware can encrypt your active files, but a clean, untouched version from before the infection remains recoverable.
 How much does a NAS cost for a small business in Canada?
 A 2-bay NAS chassis alone runs roughly $250-$450 CAD, plus about $100-$180 CAD per NAS-rated hard drive. A 4-to-5-bay model with more RAM and immutable snapshot support typically runs $600-$1,100 CAD for the chassis, plus drives. Add roughly $10-$45 CAD per month for offsite cloud replication depending on volume. In total, a 10-to-25-employee business usually sets up a complete NAS solution — chassis, drives, and cloud backup included — for an initial budget of $1,500-$3,000 CAD, plus a modest recurring monthly cost.
 Should a small business use local NAS storage or cloud backup?
 It isn't a choice between the two — combining both is what actually provides real protection. A local NAS gives fast restores for everyday needs and doesn't depend on internet speed. A cloud copy protects against theft, fire, or flooding at the office since it's physically elsewhere. The hybrid approach — a local NAS with immutable snapshots plus an encrypted offsite cloud copy — is what genuinely satisfies the 3-2-1 backup rule, and it's what we recommend to the large majority of our small business clients.
 Synology or QNAP — which should a small business choose?
 Both are reliable brands used by thousands of small businesses. Synology (DSM) generally has a simpler interface, a strong reputation for stability, and solid immutable snapshot support on recent Btrfs-based models. QNAP (QTS or QuTS hero) often offers more raw performance and flexibility for a comparable price, with ZFS support on select higher-end models, at the cost of a somewhat more technical interface. For most small businesses without in-house IT staff, Synology is usually the simpler choice; for businesses with more demanding performance needs, QNAP is often the better value per dollar.
 How does a NAS fit into the 3-2-1 backup rule?
 The 3-2-1 rule requires three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy offsite. A properly configured NAS can cover two of those three requirements on its own: it's a different media type from the original workstation (copy 2), and with snapshot replication to a secondary NAS or the cloud, it can also provide the offsite copy (copy 3). In practice: workstation (copy 1) + local NAS with immutable snapshots (copy 2) + cloud replication of the NAS (copy 3) is a complete, proven 3-2-1 architecture for a small business.

 Warranty and business support tier Compared Value-tier versus Plus/Pro-tier warranty length and enterprise support availability, since business-critical data justifies a different tier than personal use. 
 What to Look for in an NA for Small Businesses
 Key buying criteria so you get the right fit the first time.
 01 Remember every listed NAS here is diskless, budget drives separately
 The price shown for a NAS enclosure covers the hardware chassis, CPU, and RAM only, not the actual storage drives, NAS-grade drives built for 24/7 operation like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red still need to be budgeted on top, often adding $80 to $200 or more per bay depending on capacity and drive type.
 This matters because comparing NAS units purely by enclosure price without factoring in drive cost gives a misleading picture of the real total investment, a cheaper enclosure with more bays to fill can end up costing more overall than a pricier enclosure with fewer bays.
 Check whether a listing is diskless or ships with drives included, and add realistic per-bay drive costs to the enclosure price before comparing total cost across options.
 02 Weigh CPU class and RAM over bay count for real day-to-day performance
 Bay count determines maximum storage capacity, but CPU architecture (Intel, AMD, or ARM) and RAM amount determine how well the NAS actually handles real workloads, running apps, transcoding media on the fly, or serving multiple simultaneous users, and a higher bay count with a weak CPU can bottleneck performance regardless of how much raw storage it holds.
 This matters more the more the NAS will do beyond simple file storage, like Plex transcoding or running multiple docker containers, less if it's purely a basic backup target.
 Check the specific CPU model and RAM amount (and whether RAM is upgradeable) rather than choosing primarily by bay count.
 03 Understand RAID as a rebuild-time safety net, not a substitute for real backup
 RAID configurations protect against a single drive failure by letting the array rebuild from redundant data, but RAID is not a backup, it does nothing to protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a controller failure that affects the whole array at once.
 This distinction matters because treating RAID redundancy as sufficient backup protection is a common and risky misunderstanding, a real backup strategy needs a copy of critical data stored somewhere physically separate from the NAS itself.
 Check what RAID level a given NAS supports, and separately plan an actual backup strategy, ideally following a 3-2-1 approach, rather than relying on RAID redundancy alone.
 04 Match drive type (HDD vs SSD/NVMe) to your actual access pattern
 Traditional hard drives offer the lowest cost per terabyte for bulk storage like media libraries or backups, while SSD or NVMe-based NAS storage costs significantly more per terabyte but delivers much faster random access speeds, useful for frequently-accessed files, active project work, or serving as a fast cache tier.
 This matters directly based on how you'll actually use the storage, a media library accessed sequentially benefits little from SSD speed, while an active working file share benefits considerably.
 Check whether the NAS supports the drive type you need, and weigh the real cost-per-terabyte difference against how much you'll actually benefit from faster random access.
 05 Consider noise level if the NAS will run continuously in a shared living or office space
 A NAS that runs 24/7 generates continuous fan and drive noise, and that noise profile varies meaningfully between models, some use larger, slower-spinning fans that stay quiet, while others rely on smaller, faster fans that produce a persistent whine noticeable in a quiet room.
 This matters a great deal if the NAS will sit in a bedroom, living room, or shared home office rather than a dedicated closet or basement out of earshot.
 Check reviews specifically for real-world noise level mentions during continuous operation, not just idle noise, since drive activity and fan speed both increase under load.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 How many concurrent users can a small business NAS handle on gigabit Ethernet?
 A standard 1GbE connection works fine for document-heavy work with under 5 simultaneous users, but throughput per person drops noticeably once more people are transferring large files at the same time. 5GbE or 10GbE, on both the NAS and a matching switch, multiplies per-user throughput for larger or media-heavy teams.
 Do I need Active Directory integration for a small business NAS?
 Most small businesses eventually migrate from individual NAS logins to centralized directory sync as the team grows past roughly 5 users. It's useful for managing accounts at scale, but the setup is complex enough that it usually needs IT help to configure correctly the first time.
 Does the NAS itself need to be backed up?
 Most guidance treats a NAS only as a backup destination for computers, but ransomware attacks specifically targeting NAS devices are increasing. Set up cloud backup integration for the NAS's own data so a ransomware event or hardware failure doesn't destroy the only copy of your business files.
 Do I really need a UPS for a business NAS?
 Yes, treat it as a required companion purchase. A power outage that hits mid-write can corrupt a RAID array, and a USB-connected UPS lets the NAS detect the outage and shut down safely before that happens.
 What's the difference between Value-tier and Plus-tier NAS warranties?
 Value-tier models, like the Synology DS225+ or DS423 in this list, carry a shorter warranty with no enterprise support option. Plus-tier models, like the DS925+ or DS725+, offer longer coverage and an enterprise support add-on, worth the price step up for business-critical data.

 If the team is small and unlikely to grow much, a 2-bay unit like the UGREEN DXP2800 covers the basics affordably. Best NAS for Small Business 2026: Shared Storage & Backup

 Disclosure: SpeedTestHQ is reader-supported. We may earn a commission from purchases made through links on this page, at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we've tested or extensively researched. Last updated May 2026. 
 For teams of 2–20 people, a business-grade NAS handles shared file access, automated workstation backups, and local redundancy — without the per-user cost of cloud storage services.
 Cloud storage is convenient, but per-seat pricing adds up fast for a small team. A business NAS sits on your local network and gives every workstation a shared drive, automated backup, and a place to store project files — all without a monthly per-user fee. The right NAS for a small business is not just a consumer device with more bays. It needs to handle concurrent user access, integrate with existing user account systems, and keep running without attention for weeks at a time.
 This guide focuses on NAS devices that make genuine sense for teams of 2–20 people: models with strong multi-user performance, free business backup software, 10GbE upgrade paths, and the reliability features — ECC RAM, enterprise-grade drive certification, and proper RAID — that a business environment demands.
